analysis.one_liner: Allows Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: Despite 167 cosponsors, the bill never left House committees and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare's prescription drug benefit was created in 2003, the law explicitly barred the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would have deleted that ban and directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts with drug makers to get Medicare beneficiaries the lowest possible price, using the same bargaining tools the Department of Veterans Affairs uses when it buys drugs in bulk.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans, who would pay lower prices if the government negotiated on their behalf. Taxpayers would also benefit, since Medicare covers a large share of beneficiaries' drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering with negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and prescription drug plan sponsors.

Directs the Secretary to ensure beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price by negotiating with manufacturers, with authority similar to that of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, the Secretary of Defense, and other federal agencies that purchase drugs in bulk.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare revenue and prices would come under direct government negotiation for the first time. Pharmacy benefit managers and private drug plans could also see part of their price-negotiating role displaced.

drawbacks.text: The negotiating authority is modeled on the VA, which gets low prices partly by limiting which drugs it covers; giving HHS similar leverage could mean fewer drugs available on some formularies in exchange for lower prices.

Critics argued that government negotiation could squeeze manufacturer revenues and reduce investment in developing new drugs, and that private plans already negotiate prices on behalf of beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large — Medicare is one of the biggest drug buyers in the world, and other large federal purchasers like the VA negotiate far lower prices than Part D plans typically pay. The main honest trade-off is that hard bargaining usually requires the government to be willing to steer patients toward a narrower list of drugs, as the VA does. The bill left the design of that leverage to the Secretary, so its real-world savings depended on how aggressively a future administration used the authority.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their Health subcommittees in February 2005, never received a markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jo Ann Emerson introduced the bill on January 26, 2005, with seven original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and in mid-February 2005 was referred to the Health Subcommittee of each.
The bill attracted 167 cosponsors — 153 Democrats, 13 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it.
The bill died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007, without any action beyond subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation remained in force for another two years, and Medicare beneficiaries continued to pay prices set through negotiations among manufacturers, private drug plans, and pharmacy benefit managers rather than by the government.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to authorize Medicare to negotiate drug prices, leading a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 13 of 231 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Rep. Ramstad, Rep. Ross, and Rep. Wamp.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill but never reported it; it sat in the Health Subcommittee from February 2005 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which has jurisdiction over Medicare, also received the bill and never took it up beyond subcommittee referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.role: Industry group opposing Medicare price negotiation
against.what_they_did: Opposed granting Medicare authority to negotiate drug prices, defending the non-interference provision the bill would repeal.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration defended the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices, which had been enacted as part of the 2003 Medicare Modernization Act.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided: a Republican representative sponsored the bill and 13 Republicans joined 153 Democrats as cosponsors, while the Republican-controlled House leadership and committees never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation and let the government bargain directly with manufacturers, the way the VA does. Their prices and Medicare revenue would have come under direct downward pressure, so the industry's interest ran against beneficiaries who pay through premiums, copays, and taxes.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and private Medicare drug plans
industries.note: The non-interference clause the bill repeals protects the private plans' and intermediaries' role in negotiating prices on Medicare's behalf. Government negotiation could have displaced some of that role, though private plans would still have operated the benefit.
